exam-03-q01.why_correct_en: Individual liberty is a fundamental British value: people may make choices, express views and hold beliefs within the law. It is balanced by the rule of law and respect for other people's equal rights. The four groups to remember are democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, and mutual respect and tolerance.

exam-03-q02.why_correct_en: False. Wales has no established church. The Church in Wales is Anglican, but it was disestablished in 1920 and is now an independent, self-governing province. By contrast, the Church of England remains established in England.

exam-03-q03.why_correct_en: Hogmanay is the Scottish name for New Year's Eve and its celebrations. Traditions include singing Auld Lang Syne at midnight and first-footing, when the first person to enter a home after midnight is thought to bring luck. Its origins are uncertain and combine older midwinter customs with later Scottish traditions.

exam-03-q04.why_correct_en: Henry VIII wanted to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, but the Pope opposed it. England then broke with Rome through Acts of Parliament; the 1534 Act of Supremacy made the king head of the English Church. Henry still retained many traditional Catholic beliefs, so the break was not an immediate acceptance of every Protestant doctrine.

exam-03-q05.why_correct_en: The Hundred Years War is the name given to a series of conflicts between the English and French crowns from 1337 to 1453 over claims to the French throne and control of territory. It included truces, so it was not 100 years of continuous fighting; its conventional span is about 116 years.

exam-03-q06.why_correct_en: Bonnie Prince Charlie was Charles Edward Stuart. In 1745 he arrived in Scotland and, supported by some Highland clans, led a Jacobite rising to restore the Stuart dynasty. His army reached Derby before retreating and was defeated at Culloden in 1746; his escape later became part of romantic legend.

exam-03-q07.why_correct_en: Contact the local police because attempts to draw someone into extremism or terrorism may present a serious safety risk and should be handled by trained authorities. Call 999 if there is immediate danger, use 101 for a non-emergency, or use the police counter-terrorism reporting service for relevant information.

exam-03-q08.why_correct_en: False. NCS was never compulsory: it was a voluntary programme in England for young people, with activities intended to build skills and community participation. The programme ended on 31 March 2025, so this question now describes a historical programme; the tested point is that participation was voluntary.

exam-03-q09.why_correct_en: Beefeaters is the familiar name for the Yeoman Warders of the Tower of London. Their tradition developed from Tudor royal guards; today they perform ceremonial and security duties and lead tours. Modern Yeoman Warders normally have at least 22 years of military service. The origin of the nickname is uncertain.

exam-03-q10.why_correct_en: Concorde was a joint British-French project established by a 1962 agreement. It entered regular service in 1976, flew at about Mach 2 and crossed the Atlantic in roughly 3 hours 50 minutes before retirement in 2003. The question's claim that it was the world's only commercial supersonic aircraft is imprecise: the Soviet Tu-144 also carried passengers briefly in 1977-78. Britain and France remain the correct answer because they developed Concorde.

exam-03-q11.why_correct_en: Snowdonia is in Wales. The national park now officially uses its Welsh name, Eryri, and Snowdon is officially Yr Wyddfa. Yr Wyddfa is the highest mountain in Wales, while Eryri also contains Wales's largest natural lake, Llyn Tegid.

exam-03-q12.why_correct_en: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle created Sherlock Holmes. Doyle studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh, where surgeon Joseph Bell was known for making deductions from small observational details. Doyle later acknowledged Bell as an important model for Holmes in an 1892 letter.

exam-03-q13.why_correct_en: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Britain and France declared war on Germany two days later, making the invasion the immediate trigger for the Second World War in Europe. The Soviet Union then invaded Poland from the east, and Poland was overwhelmed in less than five weeks.

exam-03-q14.why_correct_en: St David, or Dewi Sant, is the patron saint of Wales. He was a sixth-century Welsh monk and church leader who founded a monastic community near today's St Davids. A famous legend says the ground rose beneath him while he preached; his remembered teaching to 'do the little things' remains closely associated with Welsh identity.

exam-03-q15.why_correct_en: True. The Lake District in north-west England is England's largest National Park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It contains England's highest mountain, Scafell Pike, and deepest lake, Wast Water. The wording is limited to England, not all parts of the UK.

exam-03-q16.why_correct_en: Theatreland is the familiar name for the concentration of commercial theatres in London's West End, particularly around Shaftesbury Avenue, Covent Garden and Leicester Square. It is not a borough with a fixed administrative boundary. The Society of West End Theatre was founded in 1908 and helped establish Theatreland's modern industry identity.

exam-03-q17.why_correct_en: The correct roles are setting the school's strategic direction and monitoring and evaluating performance. Governors provide vision, accountability and financial oversight; they do not run lessons or manage everyday staffing. For maintained schools, the three core functions cover strategy, holding the headteacher to account, and overseeing financial performance.

exam-03-q18.why_correct_en: The British government wanted the American colonies to contribute taxes after the Seven Years War. Colonists objected because they had no elected representatives in the British Parliament, producing the slogan 'No taxation without representation'. The Stamp Act, tea duties and the 1773 Boston Tea Party helped drive the colonies towards the 1776 Declaration of Independence.

exam-03-q19.why_correct_en: The Black Death reached Britain in 1348, during the Middle Ages. It was plague caused by Yersinia pestis; people at the time did not know the cause or have effective treatment. More than half of London's population may have died, and the resulting labour shortage increased surviving workers' bargaining power and wages.

exam-03-q20.why_correct_en: Emmeline Pankhurst was one of the best-known leaders of the suffragette movement. In 1903 she and others founded the Women's Social and Political Union in Manchester with the motto 'Deeds not words'. She was repeatedly imprisoned and joined hunger strikes while campaigning for women's voting rights.

exam-03-q21.why_correct_en: Cardiff is the capital and largest city of Wales. It was formally recognised as the Welsh capital in 1955. The Senedd building in Cardiff Bay makes the city a central location for Wales's devolved political institutions.

exam-03-q22.why_correct_en: Shipbuilding was one of the traditional heavy industries badly affected during the Great Depression. Coal, steel and textiles also suffered as world trade contracted. Jarrow became a symbol of the crisis after Palmer's shipyard closed in 1931 and unemployed residents marched to London in 1936 to petition for work.

exam-03-q23.why_correct_en: Sir Roger Bannister became the first person to run a mile in under four minutes on 6 May 1954 at Oxford's Iffley Road, recording 3:59.4. Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway paced him. Bannister was then a medical student; he retired from competition later that year and became a neurologist.

exam-03-q24.why_correct_en: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan and means the festival of breaking the fast. It begins in the Islamic month of Shawwal, with the date varying by the lunar calendar and moon sighting. Customs include Eid prayer, family gatherings, gifts and Zakat al-Fitr for people in need. It is distinct from Eid al-Adha, associated with sacrifice and the Hajj period.
